The neural basis of imagination: an evolutionary perspective

Episodic memory is best understood as a constructive, self-referential system for simulating particular events situated in space and time. Its signature is autonoesis-a first-person sense of "re-living"-implemented by hippocampal pattern completion over distributed cortical features, coordinated with posterior-medial (context/scene) and anterior-temporal (items/people/concepts) systems and embedded in the default mode network. Rather than storing veridical records, the system flexibly recombines stored elements to reconstruct or preconstruct episodes, which explains both the vividness of recollection and its systematic distortions, as well as the large overlap between remembering the past and imagining the future. Neuropsychology and neuroimaging converge here: hippocampal damage impairs both recollection and the ability to imagine new experiences; classic PET/fMRI show common recruitment for past and future event simulation; and contemporary accounts treat episodic memory as a generative engine for event models, not a tape recorder. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. A virtual-reality task tests how new links integrate previously separate event sequences (Figure) 16. Hippocampal sequence integration predicts improved multistep behavioral predictions (Figure).

For an intelligent agent, episodic memory serves rapid, data-efficient inference over events. In the explicit mode, it can run detailed simulations that bind sensory, conceptual, contextual, and affective features into a coherent scene; in a leaner mode, it can supply key relational constraints or values without full-blown imagery. Functionally, this enables model-based decision making (via prioritized or generative replay, hippocampal-prefrontal loops, and control-DMN coupling), supports counterfactuals and planning, seeds semantic abstraction through consolidation, and underwrites social communication by letting agents present reasons for belief grounded in first-person event models. The system usually appends a reality-monitoring tag-supported by anterior medial PFC and parietal hubs-that helps distinguish experienced from merely simulated events. Emerging "barcode" results suggest a neural mechanism for assigning event-unique indices that can be reactivated at retrieval; compelling animal data and modeling exist, with human generalization an open, exciting frontier 8, 9, 10, 11.

The episodic system appears capable of spanning the full spectrum of inference-time control. In a model-free episodic control mode, the system can retrieve "what worked last time" and directly bias choice-effectively a fast, nonparametric cache over state-action-return tuples that excels when decisions are time-pressured or environments are near-deterministic. This idea is formalized in model-free episodic control algorithms and maps naturally onto hippocampal replay mechanisms that stamp back high-return sequences. At an intermediate grain, hippocampal/entorhinal codes often look successor-like: predictive, policy-dependent state embeddings that cheaply generalize values yet are limited when transition structure changes. At the deliberative end, hippocampal-prefrontal loops use prioritized replay and prospective sweeps to support model-based planning when time and control resources allow, with lesion and fMRI work tying hippocampus to model-based choice. Together, these modes explain why EM can sometimes feel like a one-shot "do what worked," sometimes like a fuzzy but efficient look-ahead, and sometimes like explicit multistep planning 12, 13, 14, 15.
